### page_1
Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215–236
Post Jotnian basic Intrusions in the Fennoscandian Shield,
and the break up of Baltica from Laurentia: a
palaeomagnetic and AMS study
Sten-A/p44ke Elming *, Ha˚kan Mattsson
Di/p54ision of Applied Geophysics , Lulea˚U n i/p54ersity of Technology , 97187 Lulea˚, Sweden
Accepted 15 December 2000
Abstract
A palaeomagnetic and anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) study has been performed on dolerite sills of
the Central Scandinavian Dolerite Group (CSDG) in the Fennoscandian Shield. The dolerites occur in four
previously known complexes in central Sweden and Finland and from the results of this palaeomagnetic study
another complex has been identiﬁed in northern Sweden. These complexes cover an area of at least 100 000 km
2 and
the palaeomagnetic data suggest a small difference in time between the intrusion of the dolerites. The measurements
of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility reveal a magnetic fabric with almost horizontal foliation planes and lineations
that indicate fairly uniform ca NW or SE directed magma ﬂows. The dolerites of the CSDG are geochemically rather
uniform and have compositions typical of mantle derived melts formed in continental tensional settings. In a
palaeomagnetic reconstruction of Baltica versus Laurentia at ca 1.27 Ga the two continents were joined, with NE
Greenland attached to NW Baltica. AMS data from a few dolerites and a basalt in NE Greenland indicate magma
ﬂow directions that in the tectonic reconstruction are more or less parallel to the ﬂow of the dolerites in Sweden. This
may suggest a common magma source located at the reconstructed contact between Baltica and Laurentia. Both the
dolerites in Greenland and those in Sweden are of tholeitic composition indicating an intraplate origin, which
supports the interpretation of joined continents at that time. The tensional regime, that is reﬂected by the huge sill
complexes, is in our interpretation related to the break up of Baltica from Laurentia at ca 1.27 Ga ago. © 2001
Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.
Keywords: Baltica; Dolerite sills; Palaeomagnetism; Magnetic susceptibility; Geochemistry
www.elsevier.com/locate/precamres
1. Introduction
Maﬁc dykes represent an expression of crustal
extension and are the feeding channels for basaltic
magma when it is transferred from the mantle to
the upper crust. On the continents maﬁc dykes
have been intruded throughout the Proterozoic
* Corresponding author. Fax: +46-920-91697.
E-mail addresses: sten-ake.elming@sb.luth.se (S.A/p44. Elming),
hakan.mattsson@sb.luth.se (H. Mattsson).
0301-9268/01/$ - see front matter © 2001 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.
P I I : S0301-9268(01)00131-0

### page_2
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236216
and Phanerozoic. Most late Phanerozoic dyke
swarms are associated with divergent plate mar-
gins, however, some have been emplaced as a
result of plate subduction (e.g. Nakamura, 1977),
back arc spreading (Church, 1985) and collision
(Feraud et al., 1987). In the Proterozoic the asso-
ciation between dyke intrusions and plate tectonic
processes is not that clear as plate boundaries
have been affected by later collisional events.
Metamorphism and erosion of the crust make
products of Proterozoic passive margin events
difﬁcult to trace and basic dykes of this age can
therefore be more dif ﬁcult to put into a plate
tectonic context.
In the Fennoscandian Shield various genera-
tions of dyke complexes intruded the shield dur-
ing the Precambrian. At ca 1.27 Ga ma ﬁc gently
dipping sills and dykes (Welin and Lundqvist,
1975; Patchett, 1978; Suominen, 1991), the Cen-
tral Scandinavian Dolerite Group (CSDG; Gor-
batschev et al., 1979), intruded the central part of
Sweden and southwestern part of Finland, ex-
tending over an area of at least ca 100 000 km
2.
This group of ma ﬁc intrusions is coeval with large
igneous events in the North Atlantic area, e.g. the
Gardar dykes in Greenland and the Mackenzie
and Sudbury dykes in Canada. The purpose of
this study is to put these Mesoproterozoic
Fennoscandian sill complexes into a plate tectonic
framework.
Basic dykes have proven to be excellent palaeo-
magnetic recorders and consistent results have
also been reported from these sills and dykes in
Finland and Sweden (Neuvonen, 1965; Neuvonen
and Grundstro¨m, 1969; Poorter, 1976; Piper,
1979; Magnusson, 1983; Bylund, 1985). By calcu-
lating and comparing the palaeomagnetic poles
for maﬁc intrusions in various parts of the shield
we want to de ﬁne the extension of the CSDG and
we also look for eventual differences in time of
intrusion of the dolerites. Geochemical analyses
of the sills will provide information of the geolog-
ical environment at the time of intrusion and may
give constraints to plate tectonic reconstructions.
By measurement of anisotropy of magnetic sus-
ceptibility (AMS) preferred orientation of mag-
netic grains in the sills can be de ﬁned. In basic
dykes AMS measurements have shown that there
is a relation between direction of magma ﬂow and
orientation of grains (Knight and Walker, 1988).
Here we measure the AMS of the sills in an
attempt to de ﬁne the ﬂow direction of the magma
and look for eventual geographical variations.
2. Geology of the Fennoscandian Shield and
1.25 Ga dyke intrusions in Greenland and North
America
The Fennoscandian Shield is divided into a
number of tectono-magmatic blocks (Fig. 1), with
the oldest parts in the northeast. These blocks
represent a geochronological zonation and an ac-
cretionary growth of Fennoscandia during several
successive orogenic events, i.e. the Loopian (2.9 –
2.6 Ga), the Svecofennian (1.9 –1.85 Ga), the
Gothian, and the Trans-Scandinavian Granite
and Porphyry Belt (1.81 –1.5 Ga), the Sveconor-
wegian (1.25 –0.85 Ga) and the Caledonian (0.6 –
0.4 Ga) events, respectively. The Svecofennian
province forms the central part of the shield and
is divided into northern, central and southern
subprovinces (Gaal and Gorbatschev, 1987; Fig.
1). Rocks of the Trans-Scandinavian Granite and
Porphyry Belt (TGPB; Gorbatschev, 1985) and
the Gothnian orogeny truncate the Svecofennian
province in the southwest and the Southwest
Scandinavian province, which was formed during
the Gothnian orogeny and strongly reworked dur-
ing the Sveconorwegian orogeny. Large volumes
of maﬁc dykes were intruded within two different
time intervals during and after the Gothnian
orogeny. At ca 1.65 –1.3 Ga dykes associated with
anorogenic granite emplacement intruded the
crust in the central parts of the shield and at ca
1.27 Ga ma ﬁc sills and dykes of the CSDG in-
truded primarly into the southern and central
Svecofennian subprovinces and the TGPB. The
Central Scandinavian Dolerites have been divided
into four geographically separated complexes, the
Satakunta, the Ja¨mtland, the Ulvo¨ and the Dala
complexes (Fig. 1). Flat lying ma ﬁc intrusions
have been identi ﬁed in drilling and from seismic
data in deep parts of the crust beneath the Siljan
Impact Structure (Juhlin and Pedersen, 1987) and
probably also from seismic data in the basement

### page_3
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236 217
beneath the Caledonian nappes in Ja¨mtland (Palm
et al., 1991). Seismic re ﬂection data from the
Bothnian Bay also reveal several prominent re ﬂec-
tors in the crust which are interpreted as dolerite
sills (BABEL Working Group, 1993), suggesting a
more or less continuous belt of dolerites from
Sweden to Finland. The large areal extent of the
sill complexes indicates that a signi ﬁcant volume
of maﬁc magma was added to the Fennoscandian
crust. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent within
and between the different complexes (Bylund and
Pesonen, 1987), which may suggest that there wasFig. 1. The geographical distribution of sampled sites of this study (dots) and palaeomagnetic sites from previous investigations
(crosses). The various Postjotnian sill complexes are de ﬁned by the hatched lines. In the inset the tectonomagmatic block division
of the Fennoscandian Shield (modi ﬁed after Gaal and Gorbatschev, 1987; Elming et al., 1993) is shown. The numbers correspond
to the following blocks: Archaean province: (1) Kola; (2) Belomoria; and (3) Karelia subprovinces: S/p54ecofennian province: (4)
Lappland granulite belt; (5) Jatulian /Svecofennian outlier in Karelia; (6) Northern Svecofennian subprovince; (7) Skellefte and
Raahe Ladoga belts; (8) Central Svecofennian subprovince; (9) Southern Svecofennian subprovince; (10) Transscandinavian
Granite-Porphyry Belt; (11) Rapakivi granites: Southwestern Scandina /p54ian province: (12) Protogine zone; (13) Southwest Scandina-
vian subprovince; (14) Caledonides.

### page_4
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236218
little or no difference in time between the
intrusions.
Dyke swarms and sills of similar age are found
in the southern and northern parts of Greenland.
In south Greenland, in the 1.9 –1.7 Ga old
Ketilidian mobile belt, rifting took place during
the Gardar period (1.3 –1.1 Ga; Emeleus and Up-
ton, 1976). This rifting is characterized by intru-
sions of alkaline complexes and swarms of WNW
to NE trending basic to salic dykes emplaced in a
zone some 200 km long and 70 km wide. Four
generations of dykes have been recognized (BD0 –
BD3; Berthelsen and Henriksen, 1975) on the
basis of their trends. Dykes belonging to the W –E
trending BD1 group have been dated at 1.249 /p57
0.029 Ga (at Ivigtut) and 1.228 /p5729 Ga (at Ar-
suk; Rb –Sr, whole rock; Patchett et al., 1978),
which is very close to the age of the CSDG.
Palaeomagnetic data have been reported from the
different generations of dykes, from alkaline com-
plexes, lavas and sedimentary rocks (Piper, 1992;
Thomas and Piper, 1992; Piper, 1994, 1995; Piper
et al., 1998), representing ages of magnetization
from ca 1.30 to 1.16 Ga. At about 1.25 Ga intense
volcanic activity took place in eastern north
Greenland. This resulted in large sill complexes
and a sequence of tholeitic ﬂood basalts, the
Zig–Zag Dal Basalts (Kalsbeek and Jepsen,
1983). The dolerite sills and dykes have a quartz –
tholeitic composition (Jepsen, 1971; Jepsen and
Kalsbeek, 1979) and intrude Middle Proterozoic
sandstones of the Independence Fjord Group.
Hydrothermal alterations in intrusions related to
the sill complexes have Rb –Sr isochron ages of ca
1.23 Ga (Jepsen and Kalsbeek, 1979; Kalsbeek
and Jepsen, 1983). These alterations probably oc-
cured not long after the time of intrusion of the
sills (Kalsbeek and Jepsen, 1983). Palaeomagnetic
data and some AMS data have been reported
from the basalt and the sill complexes (Marcussen
and Abrahamsen, 1983).
In the Laurentian Shield the Sudbury and
Mackenzie dykes are of similar age (1.267 /p570.002
Ga; LeCheminant and Heaman, 1989 and
1.235 /p570.007/− 3; Duda`s et al., 1994, respec-
tively) as the CSDG in the Fennoscandian Shield.
The Mackenzie dykes form a huge swarm of
N–NW trending dykes in the Churchill Province
and geochemical data (Fahrig and West, 1986;
Gibson et al., 1987) suggest that they are not
related with the WNW trending Sudbury dykes in
the southern Superior Province.
3. Sampling
Samples for palaeomagnetic and AMS analyses
were collected from the CSDG complexes in
Ja¨mtland, Ulvo¨n and Satakunta areas. Samples of
sills and dykes were also taken from an area north
of ca 63 ° latitude in Sweden, where members of
the Central Scandinavian Dolerite Suite have so
far not been identi ﬁed (Fig. 1). Geochemical
analyses were made on the samples from this area
and on the samples from Ja ¨mtland.
The samples were collected with a portable drill
and as block samples and were oriented using
magnetic and sun compasses. Generally each site
represents at least 20 m
2 of outcrop. The study
includes 336 samples collected at 39 sites dis-
tributed over an area from 61.0 ° latitude and
22.17° longitude in the southeast (southwestern
Finland) to 65.73° latitude and 17.32° longitude in
the northwest (northern Sweden).
4. Palaeomagnetic results
The specimens were demagnetized by conven-
tional alternating ﬁeld and thermal demagnetiza-
tion techniques and the remanent magnetizations
were measured with a spinner (Czech-JR5) and a
SQUID (2G-DC) magnetometer. The different
components of remanence were de ﬁned by least
square ﬁtting of vectors in three-dimensional
space (Torsvik, 1986; Torsvik et al., 1996) and by
principal component analyses (Kirschvink, 1980).
The vectors were generally de ﬁned with mean
angular deviations smaller than 7 °.
It was possible to de ﬁne a characteristic magne-
tization in 38 of the 39 sampled sites.
4.1. The Ja¨ mtland complex
Dolerite sills in the Ja¨mtland area were sampled
in 15 geographically well separated sites. From

S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236 219
Fig. 2. Examples of remanence behaviour during progressive alternating ﬁeld and thermal demagnetization is shown in vector plots
of dolerite samples from: (a) the Ja ¨mtland Complex; (b) the Ulvo ¨ Complex; (c) the Satakunta Complex; and (d) sills in northern
Sweden (the Va¨sterbotten Complex). Open (closed) symbols in the vector plots denote projections in a vertical (horizontal) plane.
this complex only two sills have been studied
before (Bylund, 1985; Fig. 1Table 2). The doler-
ites often have an ophitic texture and carry large
amounts of magnetite surrounded by ilmenite
lamellae. Plagioclase, biotite, titan-rich augite and
olivine are common minerals and minor amounts
of pyrite, pyrrhotite and chalcopyrite are often
present. The sills are classi ﬁed as olivine diabases.
The Koenigsbereger-ratio ( Q-value) varies, and is
as high as 30 at some sites, however at the major-
ity it is in the range 0.62 –1.0. In 14 of the sites it
was possible to de ﬁne a characteristic magnetiza-

### page_6
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236220
tion usually isolated in a narrow range of un-
blocking temperatures of ca 560 –580°C (Fig. 2a).
The coercivity of the natural remanent magnetiza-
tion (NRM) is generally high, with median de-
structive ﬁelds (MDF; Dunlop and O /p56zdemir,
1997) of ca 20 mT (Fig. 2a). This suggests that the
carrier of remanence is predominantly pseudo-
single-domain magnetite-titanomagnetite. There is
a small portion of soft remanence, which is usu-
ally erased at l5 –20 mT demagnetizing ﬁelds. This
soft remanence carries a magnetization with a
direction similar to that of the present earth ’s ﬁeld
(PEF; Fig. 2a). Also in thermal demagnetizations
a low unblocking temperature component is iso-
lated and from the similarity in direction with that
of the PEF a viscous origin for this remanence is
suggested (Fig. 2a).
The site mean directions are fairly well de ﬁned
with precision parameters (Fisher, 1958) generally
higher than 40 (Table 1). The site mean directions
are distributed within a narrow range of declina-
tions but wide range of inclinations (Fig. 3a). This
distribution of directions is sometimes also seen
during alternating ﬁeld demagnetization of indi-
vidual samples, where components of higher nega-
tive inclinations are isolated in higher coercivity
ranges. The reason for the gradual changes in
direction is probably due to overlapping coerciv-
ity spectra, between the viscous and the primary
magnetization. Such gradual changes in directions
are also observed during thermal demagnetiza-
tion, but here the two components are clearly
separated (Fig. 2a). This means that imperfect
cleaning and isolation of the different components
of magnetization during AF demagnetizations
may explain the distribution of site mean direc-
tions. At site 29 the sill has baked the host rock,
the Ra¨tan granite (Mattsson and Elming, 2000).
In other localities in that region a characteristic
magnetization has been de ﬁned for the granite,
with a direction of magnetization signi ﬁcantly dif-
ferent from that of the sill. This suggests that the
high unblocking temperature and coercivity mag-
netization in the sills relate to a primary origin.
These site mean directions form a rather well
deﬁned mean direction of characteristic magne-
tization for the Ja ¨mtland Complex at a declina-
tion of 37.8 ° and inclination of −37.3°
(/p104
95 =9.1°; Fig. 4 Table 3).
4.2. The Ul /p54o¨ complex
Sills within the Ulvo¨ Complex have been sam-
pled at four sites. The sill at Ulvo ¨n is usually
medium grained and layered. The layering is ex-
pressed by prefered orientation of tabular plagio-
clase, and to some extent augite crystals,
subparallel with the plane of layering (Lundqvist
and Samuelsson, 1973; Larsson, 1980). The main
minerals are plagioclase, augite, olivine, biotite
and Fe –Ti oxides. This complex has earlier been
subject to extensive palaeomagnetic studies (Neu-
vonen, 1966; Poorter, 1975; Magnusson and
Larsson, 1977; Piper, 1979, 1980; Table 2). Three
of the sites in our study are located at the north-
ern and southern edges of the complex and only
one is from the more central part (Fig. 1).
The magnetic properties of these sills are simi-
lar to those of the Ja ¨mtland Complex. The coer-
civity of remanence varies from medium high to
high (MDF ’so f1 2 –26 mT; Fig. 2b) and also in
these sills a low coercivity component carries a
direction close to that of PEF. The unblocking
temperature of the characteristic magnetization is
in the range 550 –580°C and in the thermal de-
magnetizations a low unblocking temperature
component with a PEF direction can be isolated
(Fig. 2b). At site 15 the gradual change in direc-
tions during thermal demagnetization falls along
great circles that intersect (decl. =67.1, incl. =−
66.3) not very far from the mean direction de ﬁned
from the high unblocking temperature compo-
nents (decl. =49.1, incl. =− 51.7; Table 1). The
sill at this site has probably baked a rapakivi
granite, while dykes related to the rapakivi intru-
sion are not affected (Moakhar and Elming,
2000). This may indicate a primary origin of the
remanent magnetization. The site mean directions
are most often very well de ﬁned (Fig. 3b) and
they cluster around a mean for the Ulvo¨ Complex
with a declination of 48.1 ° and inclination of
−45.3° (Fig. 4; Table 3).
4.3. Satakunta complex
The sill complex in southwestern Finland cuts
Svecofennian and rapakivi rocks and Jotnian
sandstone. The dolerites have a subophitic texture

and the main minerals are plagioclase, augite,
olivine and ilmenomagnetite (Ha¨ma¨la¨inen, 1987).
Samples of the dolerites were collected in seven
sites (Fig. 1). The coercivity of remanence is high
for these sills with MDFs of 30 –40 mT and the
unblocking temperatures are restricted to a nar-
row temperature range between 560 and 580 °C
indicating that the carrier of remanence is pseudo-
single-domain magnetite-titanomagnetite. Also in
these sills the direction of remanence changes
from low negative to intermediate high inclina-
tions during AF demagnetization. A stable char-
acteristic magnetization is de ﬁned after
demagnetization in ﬁelds higher than 40 mT, with
a vector declining towards the origin in the vector
plot (Fig. 2c). The intensity of remanence in-
creases during the ﬁrst steps of demagnetization
and in the very low coercivity range it is possible
to isolate a remanence component with a direc-
tion of positive inclination not far from that of
the PEF (Fig. 2c). This explains the gradual
change of direction of the remanence vector dur-
ing progressive demagnetization, similar to what
has been observed for sills in other parts of the
shield (e.g. in the Section 4.1).
The mean directions of characteristic magne-
tizations at the different sites are well de ﬁned with
precission parameters (Fisher, 1958) higher than
43 (Table 1) and they form a tight cluster around
a mean direction for the Finnish sills at 44.7 °
declination and −40.3° inclination (Fig. 4; Table
3).
On the Swedish side of the Bothnian Bay a
basic dyke and a sill (sites 30 and 31; Fig. 1)
probably belonging to the CSDG were studied.
The MDFs are high for both of them varying
between ca 25 and 35 mT and characteristic mag-
netizations were isolated in demagnetizing ﬁelds
of 30 mT and higher (Fig. 2c). Also in these
dolerites a soft remanence with a direction similar

4.4. The Va¨ sterbotten complex , northern Sweden
Dolerite sills in northern Sweden have been
sampled at 11 sites (Fig. 1). On the basis of
microscope studies the sills are classi ﬁed as olivine
diabases and are medium to ﬁne grained with
subophitic to ophitic texture. The magnetite has a
primary character and occurs mainly in composite
grains with ilmenite lamellae. Small amounts of
pyrite and sometimes pyrrhotite are often ob-
served. A characteristic magnetization is usually
isolated in a narrow range of unblocking tempera-
tures of ca 560 –580°C (Fig. 2d). The coercivities
of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM)
vary, but are generally high, with MDF ’so fc a2 5
mT (Fig. 2d). This suggests that the carrier of
remanence in these sills is predominately pseudo-
single-domain magnetite-titanomagnetite. The
samples with a larger portion of low coercivity
remanence carry a magnetization with a direction
similar to that of the present earth ﬁeld (PEF). In
these samples a characteristic remanence is often
isolated in alternating ﬁelds higher than 25 mT. In
sills where the NRM is mainly carried by pseudo-
single-domain grains there is only a small portion
of soft remanence, which is erased at 5 –10 mT
to that of PEF could be removed in demagnetiz-
ing ﬁelds of 10 –15 mT. The mean directions of
the characteristic magnetizations (site 30: decl. =
24.7, incl. =− 16.9 and site 31: decl. =11.3,
incl.=− 19.2; Fig. 4; Table 1) are however quite
different when compared to the sills from Finland
(Fig. 3c) and are not combined with those to
derive a mean of the complex.

demagnetizing ﬁelds (Fig. 2d). Also in thermal
demagnetizations low unblocking temperature
components are isolated and from the similarity
in direction with that of the PEF a viscous origin
for this remanence is suggested.
The site mean directions are fairly well de ﬁned
and for a majority of sites the precission parame-
ter is higher than 30 (Table 1). Apart from the
mean direction of site 11 (Table 1; Fig. 3d) the
site mean directions cluster around a mean direc-
tion for these sills at 45.0 ° declination and −
45.0° inclination (Table 3; Fig. 4). If site 11 is
included the mean direction does not change sig-
niﬁcantly (decl. =41.5°, incl. =− 43.2°), although
the precision of the mean decreases (Table 3).
5. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility
The anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility
(AMS) was measured to de ﬁne the magnetic fab-
ric of the sills at 35 of the sites. Two dolerite
dykes that cut sills of the Ulvo ¨ Complex (sites
14a, c; Fig. 1) were also included in the study. On
average nine samples from each site were mea-
sured. Basically, the AMS of a rock is described
by a second-order tensor (e.g. Hrouda, 1982),
which can be visualized by an ellipsoid with three
principal axes of maximum, intermediate and
minimum susceptibility ( k
max, kint and kmin, re-
spectively). For multi-domain magnetite the kmax
axis is parallel to the long axis of an ellipsoidal
grain and for most rocks the kmax corresponds to
the mineral lineation, whereas the kmin axis corre-
sponds to the pole of the plane of magnetic
foliation (Tarling and Hrouda, 1993). The degree
of anisotropy is characterized by P=k
max/kmin
and the shape of the anisotropy ellipsoid is
deﬁned by the shape parameter T (Jelı´nek, 1981).
For −1/p66T/p660 the ellipsoid is prolate (cigar-
shaped) and for 0 /p66T/p661 the ellipsoid is oblate
(disc-shaped). If T=0 the ellipsoid is neutral. The
AMS and temperature variation of magnetic sus-
ceptibility of rocks were measured with a Kap-
pabridge KLY-3 and a CS-3 instrument,
respectively (Geofyzika Brno). The statistical
analysis of the AMS data was performed using a
technique of Jel ı´nek (1978).
It is believed that elongated particles in a ﬂow-
ing magma become imbricated along the dyke
margin and when the magma crystallizes the ox-
ides will mimic the fabric of the preexisting silicate
phases (Tauxe et al., 1998). If ferromagnetic
grains of multi-domain size dominate the mag-
netic susceptibility of the rock the preferred orien-
tation of the k
max axis will be parallel to the ﬂow
direction of the magma. Since Knight and Walker
(1988) demonstrated the use of AMS as an indica-
tor of direction of magma ﬂow in dykes the
method has been used in several studies to de ﬁne
ﬂow fabrics (e.g. Bates and Mushayandebvu,
1995; Raposo, 1997). Dragoni et al. (1997) pre-
sented a theoretical model for the behavior of
rigid ellipsoidal grains in a ﬂowing magma driven
by a pressure gradient. They compared the model
results with AMS fabrics from Ferrar dolerite sills
on east Antarctica and concluded that the mag-
netic lineation is generally a good marker of the
magma ﬂow direction. The exception was in the
center of the sill body which is essentially strain-
free and no preferred orientation can be de ﬁned.
Large scatter or absence of preferred directions in
the magnetic lineations may thus indicate that the
measured samples were not collected close to the
sill margin.
In our study we could only in rare cases ob-
serve the contact between the host rock and the
sill and it is thus not possible to determine where
in the sill body the samples were collected. On
basis of statistical requirements for the con ﬁdence
of mean AMS directions (Jel ı´nek, 1978) a maxi-
mum size limit for the semi axes of the 95%
conﬁdence ellipse of the mean lineation direction
is set to 25 °. Sites that have mean directions with
conﬁdence ellipses above this limit are considered
to poorly de ﬁned to represent a statistically reli-
able direction, and are therefore rejected.
5.1. Results of the AMS study
The degree of anisotropy is generally below
10% for the sills and dykes in this study (on
average P=1.05; Fig. 5b, c; Table 4), which is the
usual for igneous rocks with a primary magnetic
fabric (Hrouda, 1982). The site mean susceptibil-
ity average is 31 ×10
−3 SI, ranging from 13.7 ×

### page_12
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236226
Fig. 5. Anisotropy parameters of: (a) the dolerite sills; (b) Histogram of the mean susceptibility for all specimens ( n=434); (b) the
shape parameter T plotted as a function of the degree of anisotropy for the sills in northern Sweden, the Ja ¨mtland and the Ulvo¨
complexes ( n=339); (c) the shape parameter T plotted as a function of the degree of anisotropy for the Satakunta Complex
(including site 31; n=95).
10−3 (site 19) to 80.4 ×10−3 SI (site 14a) (Fig.
5a; Table 4). Susceptibility –temperature data in-
dicate that magnetite or titano-magnetite is the
main carrier of the susceptibility of the sills. No
signiﬁcant differences in susceptibility or an-
isotropy parameters are found between the three
rock-complexes in Sweden (Va ¨stebotten, Ulvo¨n
and Ja¨mtland). A majority of the specimens have
oblate shape anisotropy ellipsoids, but there are
examples of specimens with strongly developed
prolate shaped ellipsoids as well (Fig. 5b). At the
Satakunta Complex the ellipsoids have stronger
developed oblate shape and only four of the 69
samples have dominant prolate shaped ellipsoids
(Fig. 5c). The average degree of lineation is
slightly lower for the Satakunta Complex ( L=
1.008) than for the Va ¨sterbotten ( L=1.012), Ul-
vo¨n( L=1.012) and Ja ¨mtland ( L=1.011)
complexes, however, the differences are not statis-
tically signi ﬁcant. The minimum anisotropy axes
in the sills of all the four complexes are, with few
exceptions, clustered in subvertical directions and
the magnetic foliation planes have an average dip
of 13 °. One exception from this pattern of distri-
bution is found at the site 26 (Fig. 1) where there
is a tendency for a girdle distribution of the k
min
axes, which may indicate that the grains under-
went rotation during the magma ﬂow. However,
at site 26 the sill has a deviating remanence direc-
tion, probably indicating a post intrusion tectonic
disturbance. The maximum and intermediate axes
are often distributed in a subhorizontal girdle
pattern, which makes it more dif ﬁcult to de ﬁne a
reliable mean direction of the lineation (Fig. 6).
At 15 of the 35 sites the de ﬁned mean directions
of lineation satisfy our statistical demands, which
means that they have semi-angles of the 95%
conﬁdence ellipses that are smaller than 25 °
(Table 4). At site 14 in the Ulvo ¨ Complex three
localities were sampled and at two of them it was
possible to de ﬁne a reliable direction of lineation.
The dif ﬁculty of de ﬁning statistically reliable di-
rections of lineation is to some extent caused by
the limited number of samples. However, in many
cases it most likely indicates a true absence of
preferred direction of lineation, i.e. the samples
may have been collected from the central, strain
free part, of the sometimes 250 m thick sill body,
where no preferred direction exists (Dragoni et
al., 1997). Plotting the directions of sample lin-
eation for each complex on an equal area net the
contour plots (Fig. 7) generally indicates a girdle
distribution of the lineation at the Ulvo¨,J a¨mtland
and Satakunta complexes, however, with clusters
of directions. In the Va ¨sterbotten Complex the
directions are less scattered and the clusters are in
NNW–SSE to NW –SE trending directions.
These trends of the magnetic lineation in the
Va¨sterbotten sills are also expressed in the mean
directions of the sites and NW –SE directions
dominate. These directions roughly coincide with
the NNW –SSE to NNE –SSW trending lineations

### page_13
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236 227
of the Ulvo ¨ complex located southeast of the
Va¨sterbotten Complex (Fig. 8). A NW –SE trend
is also dominant in the Ja¨mtland Complex further
to the southwest, however, there is one site with a
mean lineation directed NNE –SSW. In the Sa-
takunta Complex in Finland, the situation is
slightly different. Signi ﬁcant mean directions of
lineation can be determined in four of the seven
sites. In three of these sites the lineations trend in
NNE–SSW directions, while in the fourth site the
lineation trend is NW –SE (Fig. 8).
We interpret the AMS data as a primary ﬂow
fabric indicator of the rocks at all 35 sites. A ﬂow
origin is supported by AMS data from a sill in the

Fig. 6. Examples of directions of the maximum ( ﬁlled squares) and minimum (dots) anisotropy axes of susceptibility in sills from:
(a) the Ja¨mtland Complex; (b) the Ulvo¨ Complex; (c) the Satakunta Complex; and (d) the northern Sweden sills. The directions are

Ja¨mtland complex (site 20) that cuts a deforma-
tion zone. While the host rock is deformed and
has a susceptibility anisotropy with a vertical
foliation plane corresponding to the deformation-
related mineral fabric, the anisotropy of the sill
exhibits a magnetic foliation plane parallel to the
plane of the sill. A ﬂow origin is also supported
by the preferred orientation of plagioclase crystals
in the layered sill at Ulvo ¨n.
The two dykes at Ulvo ¨n (sites 14a and c) are
subvertical and strike WNW (site 14a) and north
(site 14c). It is suggested that both dykes carry a
primary AMS fabric since the degree of an-
isotropy is less than 10%. The magnetic lineation
of the dykes clusters subhorizontally, which indi-
cates that the dykes were fed by horizontal ﬂuxes
and that Ulvo¨n was situated far from the magma
source at the time of emplacement (Raposo,
1997). The inferred ﬂow direction of the sill at site
14a is NNW –SSE and ca 45 ° away from the
trend of the cutting dyke. This may indicate that
the two rocks were emplaced at different times
and under different stress conditions.
6. Geochemistry
In 32 samples from Va ¨sterbotten and 13 from
Ja¨mtland, major and trace elements were analysed
by SGAB Analytica in Lulea ˚ by using ICP-AES.
Apart from the new chemical analyses, there are
previously presented analyses from the Ja ¨mtland
area (Gorbatschev et al., 1979), from the Ulvo ¨
area (Lundqvist and Samuelsson, 1973; Larsson,
1980; Thomas Lundqvist, 2000, unpublished
analyses) and from the Satakunta area
(Ha¨ma¨la¨inen, 1987).
The CSDG rocks are not much altered, and
have largely kept their primary mineralogy. The
basic intrusions in Va¨sterbotten, Ja¨mtland, Ulvo¨n
and Satakunta areas all have similar tholeitic
compositions, which indicate an intraplate origin.

### page_15
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236 229
7. Discussion
The mean remanence directions (Figs. 3 and 4)
and the calculated palaeomagnetic pole positions
(Fig. 9a and b; Table 3) of the sills from the Ulvo¨,
the Ja¨mtland and the Satakunta complexes in this
study are not signi ﬁcantly different. The same is
true when our new data are combined with old
data from these complexes and compared also
with the Dala Complex (Tables 2 and 3). The
similarity in palaeomagnetic directions between
these complexes was also observed by Bylund and
Pesonen (1987), however their observations were
based on a smaller amount of data, especially in
the case of the Ja ¨mtland Complex. The new
palaeomagnetic data from the northern part of
Sweden, the Va ¨sterbotten Complex (site 1 –11),
fall into the same pattern and the mean direction
and mean pole for these sills (site 11 not included)
are not signi ﬁcantly different from those of the
other complexes (Figs. 4 and 9b). This means that
the Central Scandinavian Dolerites are not re-
stricted to the central part of the shield but have
intruded the crust as far north as 65.7 ° latitude.
Up to now we have not identi ﬁed dolerites of this
magnetization age north of the Skellefte district,
which marks a boundary between the northern
and central Svecofennian subprovinces (Fig. 1).
The similarity in pole positions also means that
the sills of the different complexes were most
likely intruded within a quite narrow time inter-
val, unless there was little or no polar wander at
this time. However, the polarity of the remanence
is the same for all complexes, which argue for a
narrow time interval of the intrusions.
The mean remanence directions from three sills
(sites 11, 30 and 31) form a group of similar
directions with a mean (decl. =17.0°, incl. =−
Fig. 7. An equal area plot of the directions of magnetic lineation (maximum axis) in dolerite samples from: (a) the Ja ¨mtland
Complex; (b) the Ulvo ¨ Complex; (c) the Satakunta Complex; and (d) northern Sweden sills (the Va ¨sterbotten Complex). The
directions are shown in a downward projection.

### page_16
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236230
Fig. 8. Site mean strike directions of the magnetic lineation from 15 sites, where the directions could be de ﬁned with a radius of the
cone of con ﬁdence less than 25 °. The dip of the lineation is most often close to zero and is not accounted for in the ﬁgure.
19.0°, Table 3) signi ﬁcantly different from the
mean directions of all other sills. The geochemical
data show a signiﬁcantly different composition for
the sill at site 11, which means that the difference
in remanence directions is probably due to a
different origin and age of these dolerites. The
calculated pole (Plat. =17.2°, Plon. =179.7°,
Table 3, Fig. 9b) coincides with the ca 1.3 Ga
reference pole for the Fennoscandian Shield (Elm-
ing et al., 1993), and indicates that they may be
older than the CSDG.
The pole calculated from the sill at site 26 in the
Ja¨mtland Complex is located at an anomalously
high southern latitude (Fig. 9a). This sill also has

### page_17
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236 231
Fig. 9. (a) Site mean virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) positions plotted together with A95, the half-angle of the 95% circle of con ﬁdence. The pole at a high southern
latitude is calculated from the anomalous site 26; (b) Mean VGP position accompanied by A95 for the dolerites of: (1) the Ja¨mtland Complex; (2) the Ulvo¨ Complex;

### page_18
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236232
anomalous AMS directions, which may suggest
that it is tectonically disturbed.
The magnetic fabric data indicate a fairly uni-
form ca NW or SE directed magma ﬂow of the
dolerite sills in northern and central Sweden (the
Va¨sterbotten, Ja¨mtland and Ulvo¨ complexes, see
Fig. 8). These sites also have similar signatures of
the anisotropy parameters, which may indicate
that the magma ﬂows were formed under similar
physical conditions. The CSDG rocks have in-
truded into a much older bedrock, and the geo-
chemical data indicate a clear within-plate setting.
The similarity in geochemical composition, also
suggests that the magma came from the same
source. This source may have been located in the
central part of the shield or N –NWof the Va¨ster-
botten Complex as indicated from the magnetic
lineations. The horizontal lineation in the dykes
of the Ulvo¨ Complex suggests that the source of
magma was located far from these dykes.
The mean trend of the magnetic lineation of the
Satakunta Complex (Finland) indicates a magma
ﬂow in predominantly a NNE –SSW direction
(Fig. 8). This may suggest that the magma of the
Satakunta area comes from a different source
when compared with the other complexes, how-
ever, their chemical compositions are similar.
AMS measurements were previously performed
on the ca 1.25 Ga old Midsommerso ¨ dolerite sills
and the Zig –Zag Basalt in northeastern Green-
land (Marcussen and Abrahamsen, 1983). The
basalt is a tholeitic ﬂood basalt and the dolerites
have a quartz-tholeitic composition. Kalsbeek and
Jepsen (1983) reported some major element analy-
ses of the Midsommerso ¨ dolerites. Except for
fractionation effects, these dolerites show a wide
variation in chemical composition due to both
hydrothermal alteration and assimilation of the
wall rock. This makes a detailed comparison of
the composition of these dolerites with those from
the Baltic Shield dif ﬁcult. At three sites in the
basalt well de ﬁned susceptibility axes were deter-
mined. The minimum axes of anisotropy are gen-
erally vertical for the basalt, indicating horizontal
ﬂow, and the maximum axes are in a NE –SW
direction, which is interpreted to re ﬂect the ﬂow
direction of the magma. At two localities in the
Midsommerso¨ dolerite (locality 3; Marcussen and
Fig. 10. Tectonic reconstruction of Laurentia and Baltica at
1.27 Ga based on palaeomagnetic data and geological criteria
(Buchan et al., 2000). The arrows denote the ﬂow direction of
magma in the sills in Fennoscandia (fulldrawn line) and
Greenland (hatched line) as indicated from AMS and geologi-
cal data. Note that the ﬂows are more or less parallel and
perpendicular to the contact between Fennoscandia and
Greenland.
Abrahamsen, 1983) consistent AMS results were
obtained. In one feeder dyke the mean maximum
AMS-axis trends in a NE –SW direction (215 ° E)
and the ﬂow plane is dipping ca 42 ° to the south-
west and parallel to the dip of the dyke (40 ° SW).
In another, almost horizontal (5 –10° SW dip)
dyke, the maximum anisotropy axes are also di-
rected NE –SW (229 °). According to the authors
these results are in excellent agreement with geo-
logical evidence for the ﬂow direction and the dip
of the ﬂow plane. In three other sites from a
major sill well de ﬁned anisotropy axes with al-
most vertical maximum axes were de ﬁned, which
indicate a vertical ﬂow.
On basis of key palaeomagnetic poles for Lau-
rentia and Baltica Buchan et al. (2000) presented
a possible location of northern Baltica adjacent to
northeastern Greenland at ca 1.27 Ga (Fig. 10).
In this reconstruction the 1.8 –1.5 Ga old Gothian
and Labradorian belts are aligned and Laurentia
and Baltica may have been joined in this time

### page_19
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236 233
period. The key pole for Baltica is based on
palaeomagnetic data from the Central Scandina-
vian Dolerites and this key pole (Plat. =4°,
Plon. =158°, A
95 =4°) is not signi ﬁcantly differ-
ent from the mean pole of the sills in our study
(Plat. =− 3.8°, Plon. =159.3°, A
95 =5.6; Table
3). Laurentian key poles of corresponding age are
deﬁned from the Mackenzie and Sudbury dykes,
while there are no key poles of this age from
Greenland. However, when the position of Green-
land is reconstructed to northwestern North
America using a Mesozoic ﬁt (Roest and Srivis-
tava, 1989) the pole of the ca 1.25 Ga Gardar
dykes falls near the 1.267 Ga Mackenzie and the
1.235 Ga Sudbury poles. In this reconstruction
the poles of the Midsommero ¨ dolerites and the
Zig–Zag basalts are also similar to those of the
Laurentian key poles (Buchan et al., 2000). The
polarity of remanences in the Midsommero¨ doler-
ites and the Zig –Zag basalts are the same but
opposite to what has been de ﬁned for dykes of
similar age in central North Greenland (Abra-
hamsen and Van der Voo, 1987). Poles calculated
for the ca 1.15 Ga old Late Gardar dykes fall in
a similar way close to the poles of the 1.14 Ga
Abitibi dykes and the Logan sill for Laurentia,
which suggests that Greenland formed a part of
Laurentia at that time.
To ﬁt the reconstruction of Buchan et al. (2000)
Laurentia has to be rotated clockwise and Baltica
counterclockwise relative to their present posi-
tions (Fig. 10). In that reconstruction the polarity
of remanences of the Midsommero ¨ dolerites and
the Zig –Zag basalts is opposite to that of the
CSDG in Fennoscandia. The reconstruction sug-
gests that northeastern Greenland may have been
attached to the northwestern part of Baltica not
far from where the Va ¨sterbotten sills crop out.
The predominantly NW –SE lineation of the mag-
netic susceptibility in the Swedish sill complexes
will in this reconstruction be more or less parallel
to the corresponding lineation and proposed
magma ﬂow in the sills of similar age in north-
eastern Greenland. Marcussen and Abrahamsen
(1983) suggested, on basis of geological and AMS
data, that the ﬂow of the magma in Greenland
may have been from the NE to the SW and in one
sill vertical, that is a ﬂow from the coast towards
the interior of Greenland.
This means that the magma source should have
been located close to the coast or just outside
present day Greenland. Such a location of the
source also ﬁts into the ﬂow pattern in Baltica on
the tectonic reconstruction (Fig. 10). The parallel
ﬂow directions in the sills in northwestern and
western Baltica and the basalt and sills in north-
eastern Greenland suggest a common magma
source. The sills in Greenland and those in Baltica
are of tholeitic composition indicating an in-
traplate origin, and support the interpretation of
joined continents at that time. The location of a
magma source in the reconstructed contact be-
tween Baltica and Laurentia may be a sign of
riﬂing that re ﬂects the break up of the Baltica /
Laurentia supercontinent. The tensional regime
that is indicated by the huge sill complexes in
Baltica would then be a result of this plate tec-
tonic event.
8. Conclusion
The Central Scandinavian Dolerites represented
by the Va¨sterbotten, Ulvo¨,J a¨mtland, Satakunta
and Dalarna complexes cover more than 100 000
km
2 in the Fennoscandian Shield. Geochemically
the dolerites are rather uniform and have a com-
position typical of mantle derived melts formed in
continental tensional settings. Palaeomagnetic
data suggest a small time difference between the
intrusion of the dolerites. In a palaeomagnetic
reconstruction of Baltic a versus Laurentia at ca
1.27 Ga the two continents were joined to each
other, with NE Greenland attached to NW
Baltica. Measurements of the anisotropy of mag-
netic susceptibility show a magnetic fabric that
indicates a fairly uniform ca NW or SE directed
magma ﬂow in the dolerites in northern and
central Sweden. Corresponding measurements on
basalts and dolerites in NE Greenland indicate a
SW ﬂow direction, which in the tectonic recon-
struction of Laurentia and Baltica is parallel to
the ﬂow direction of the sills in Sweden. This may
suggest a common magma source located in the
reconstructed contact between the two continents.
Both the sills in Greenland and those in Sweden
are of tholeitic composition indicating an in-

### page_20
S.A/p44. Elming, H. Mattsson / Precambrian Research 108 (2001) 215 –236234
traplate origin, which supports the interpretation
of joined continents at that time. The tensional
regime, that is indicated by the huge sill com-
plexes, reﬂects, in our interpretation, the break up
of Baltica from Laurentia at ca 1.27 Ga ago.
